title: Verifier‑Assisted versus LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We measured whether integrating a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier (with at most one automated repair) increases the fraction of intent‑driven configuration proposals that pass semantic validation compared with accepting a single LLM candidate. In a preregistered paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) we executed 300 paired intents (100 per difficulty stratum) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic NetOps validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Each pair evaluated a single shared_initial LLM candidate under two conditions: baseline (accept single shot) and guarded (deterministic validation and ≤1 automated repair). Results: baseline 299/300 unflagged passes (0.9966667), guarded 300/300 (1.0); paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00,0.01] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Under the supplied synthetic suite and model, single‑shot generation was near ceiling, limiting observable marginal rescue by the guarded pipeline. All preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts are archived with the study id to support replication and follow‑up experiments that vary estimand conditioning, model strength, or repair budget.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are being actively applied to network operations (NetOps) for intent→configuration translation, template synthesis, and automated repair. Operators require semantic guarantees—sequencing, reachability, and policy preservation—that go beyond syntactic formatting. Tool‑augmented workflows that place deterministic validators and bounded automated repair after generation have been proposed to reduce operational risk. However, the practical rescue that such validators provide depends on the estimand (what is held fixed), model strength, validator expressiveness, and repair budget. We preregistered a paired experiment that isolates the verifier/repair effect for the same LLM candidate: for each intent we generated one shared_initial candidate with gpt-5-mini and then compared (a) accepting that candidate unmodified (baseline) versus (b) validating and permitting ≤1 deterministic automatic repair (guarded). The central research question is: does adding a deterministic verifier plus at most one automated repair increase the probability that a single LLM candidate passes semantic pre‑deployment validation compared with accepting the same single candidate without repair? Our contributions are (1) a preregistered paired evaluation (N=300) conditioned on shared_initial candidates that isolates deterministic rescue utility; (2) a fully archived execution and analysis bundle with deterministic validator traces and a representative repaired episode; and (3) empirically grounded interpretation and operational guidance about estimand choice, near‑ceiling inference behavior, and reproducibility.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and system papers document active efforts to apply LLMs to NetOps tasks and to scaffold generation with external tools and validators. Work on intent‑based translation, template synthesis, and zero‑touch workflows demonstrates feasibility but reports widely varying correctness rates depending on dataset and validator coverage [https://openalex.org/W4406484968, https://openalex.org/W4411015066, https://openalex.org/W4403635865]. Planner‑centric and ReAct‑style tool‑augmented frameworks explicitly call external validators and orchestrate repairs, motivating generate→validate→repair architectures [doi:10.1609/aaai.v40i40.40676, https://openalex.org/W4389518608]. Prior empirical reports indicate that validation and repair can reduce errors when the validator checks the operational invariants of interest [https://openalex.org/W4416927413, https://openalex.org/W4404240614], but head‑to‑head controlled comparisons that isolate deterministic rescue for the same generated candidate are scarce. Our study complements existing work by conditioning on the same LLM candidate per intent, thereby separating deterministic validator/repair rescue from effects arising from drawing additional independent candidates or iterative candidate‑generation scaffolds.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered study cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001 and froze the primary estimand: the absolute paired difference in the unflagged verifier‑pass proportion (guarded minus baseline) computed on paired cases where both conditions evaluate the same shared_initial candidate. The preregistration specified design, inclusion/exclusion rules, analysis executor, multiplicity plan, and reproducible executor inputs.

Task generation and difficulty strata. The task suite (synthetic_topology_suite_v1) was generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Tasks were stratified into low/medium/high difficulty (100 tasks per stratum) by generator difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count). Example patterns include "shutdown_configure_restore" (medium) and "paired_link_atomic_mtu_change" (hard). Representative task manifests and six example responses are archived in the execution bundle.

Modeling and orchestration. The declared model was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). To isolate rescue of the same model output, each pair used a single shared_initial generation; the guarded condition reuses that candidate and runs the deterministic validator, while baseline accepts it with no repair.

Validator, scoring rules, and repair policy. The deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implemented the preregistered full_intent_constraint_validation rule: it deterministically checks sequencing constraints (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields), reachability/policy invariants, preserved fields, and mandatory required_command_count. For guarded episodes, if the validator flagged the candidate, the pipeline permitted at most one automated repair invocation (repair budget ≤1) and then revalidated. Scoring is binary per preregistered rules: unflagged == pass; flagged after allowed repair == failure. The single rescued episode diagnostic and validator trace are archived; the repair corrected a sequencing omission (missing 'admin down' step) and restored a valid sequencing order.

Design accounting, exclusions, and pilot. The preregistration planned a pilot (n=60) to estimate discordance and calibrate power; the pilot was not executed and no post‑preregistration sample recalculation was performed. The confirmatory main run followed the frozen plan: planned_episode_count = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions), maximum_model_calls = 600, and the missingness/exclusion rules only allowed pair exclusion when both calls failed due to provider/infrastructure outage. No pairs were excluded. The preregistration's multiplicity plan treats the primary test as single confirmatory hypothesis; subgroup analyses are exploratory with Benjamini–Hochberg correction when applied.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter completed the confirmatory run: completed_episode_count = 600, complete_pair_count = 300, and model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared_initial + 1 repair). Deterministic reconciliation recorded stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and cache_miss_count = 301. No provider outages, failed episodes, or unscorable episodes were recorded (analysis/missingness_summary.csv). The contamination summary is empty.

Primary margins and contingency. Condition margins (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 299/300 (0.9966667), guarded successes = 300/300 (1.0). The paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 299, n10 = 1 (guarded‑only), n01 = 0 (baseline‑only), n00 = 0. Confirmatory inference used the preregistered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor (exact two‑sided McNemar equivalent) and produced an absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333, exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0, and a 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00,0.01] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Per‑stratum outcomes: low = 100/100 baseline and guarded, medium = 100/100 baseline and guarded, high = baseline 99/100 vs guarded 100/100.

Rescue diagnostic. The single discordant (n10) episode invoked the permitted automated repair (repair stage_count = 1). The archived validator trace attributes the initial flag to a must_be_down_for_fields sequencing violation: the shared_initial candidate omitted the required 'admin down' prior to a VLAN/MTU change. The automated repair inserted the missing sequencing command, after which the validator returned valid == true. We report this concise semantic repair summary here; the full low‑level repair provider trace and validator trace are archived in the run bundle for forensic inspection.

Inferential interpretation. The near‑ceiling baseline limited the number of discordant pairs (m = n10 + n01 = 1), so the exact McNemar test yields p = 1.0. This null discordance reflects insufficient discordant evidence under the shared_initial estimand rather than conclusive equivalence across broader operational settings. The paired bootstrap percentile CI bounds the plausible absolute paired improvement under the experimental context to at most 1 percentage point.
sections.discussion:
Near‑ceiling baseline and statistical power. When the baseline single‑shot pass rate approaches 100%, the number of discordant pairs—rather than total N—drives inferential sensitivity. Our preregistered power target (detecting a 10 percentage‑point absolute paired improvement) assumed appreciable baseline discordance; with 299/300 baseline passes, detectable improvements are tightly bounded and practical power is limited. The preregistered pilot for discordance estimation was not executed; had it been run and shown low discordance, the design could have been amended prior to main execution per preregistered amendment rules.

Estimand consequences and operational meaning. The shared_initial design intentionally isolates deterministic repair utility for a single candidate draw per intent: it answers the operational question relevant to organizations that run a single model call and then apply a deterministic validator + bounded repair as an audit/repair layer. It does not capture benefits achievable by allowing independent alternative LLM draws per arm (e.g., verifier‑guided resampling, iterative candidate generation, or model steering). In deployments where multiple model draws or interactive candidate steering are permitted, verifier benefits may be larger than observed here.

Validator coverage and failure modes. The deterministic validator checks sequencing, field‑level requirements, and policy invariants defined by full_intent_constraint_validation. The single observed failure class was sequencing omission (must_be_down_for_fields). Other failure modes that the validator is designed to detect (reachability violations, disallowed field changes, or forbidden-template modifications) were not triggered in the sampled synthetic suite at scale. This does not imply absence of such failures in realistic networks—rather, it highlights the interaction between generator difficulty sampling and validator coverage.

Operational recommendations. For practitioners: when selecting an audit/repair scaffold, explicitly define the operational estimand (shared_initial vs. resampling) that matches organizational workflows. If single model draws are standard, a bounded verifier+repair provides deterministic audit logs and can correct localized sequencing omissions, as the rescued episode here demonstrates. If larger marginal safety improvements are required, prefer designs that either (a) allow multiple independent candidate draws with verifier selection, (b) expand repair budgets to iterative repairs, or (c) evaluate weaker LLMs or tasks sampled from realistic operator incident distributions. The archived artifacts enable these follow‑ups without fabricating new data.

Reproducibility, transparency, and artifact grounding. All raw outputs, provider traces, task manifests, validator traces, analysis CSVs (analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/missingness_summary.csv), and reconciliation logs are archived under the preregistration id. The analysis executor parameters (bootstrap resamples, seed = 1729) and the exact inference methods are recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. Deterministic reconciliation confirms episode accounting and provider call audit counts; these artifacts permit exact replication of the confirmatory calculations by an independent executor.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired comparison between a verifier‑assisted pipeline (deterministic validator + ≤1 automated repair) and accepting a single‑shot LLM candidate under the shared_initial estimand on 300 synthetic NetOps intents using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Baseline single‑shot generation produced 299/300 unflagged verifier passes and the guarded pipeline 300/300, yielding an absolute paired improvement of 0.00333 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.01]). The near‑ceiling baseline limits inferential sensitivity for small absolute improvements under the shared_initial estimand. We release the preregistration id, execution and analysis artifacts, representative task manifests, and validator traces in the archived run bundle to enable reproducible follow‑ups that vary estimand choice, model strength, or repair strategies.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were generated by the preregistered deterministic task generator; real‑world heterogeneity may expose different failure modes and increase verifier marginal utility.
Single model and validator: only gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 were evaluated; results may not generalize to other LLMs or richer/diverse validators.

Ceiling effect: baseline single‑shot performance was near 100% on this suite (299/300), producing limited discordance and reduced power to detect small absolute improvements relative to larger pre‑specified targets.
Pilot not executed: the preregistered pilot intended for discordance estimation and power calibration was not run; no post‑preregistration power recalculation was performed.

Estimand conditioning: the shared_initial protocol conditions the estimand on a single LLM candidate and therefore does not measure verifier benefit that would arise from allowing independent alternative LLM candidates per condition.
Repair budget: the guarded condition permitted at most one automated repair per pair; larger or iterative repair strategies may yield different outcomes.
